doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Nat King Cole standing to sing in a noisy supper club, and sponsor racism
summary: She heard Cole as pianist on records and saw him singing in a noisy New York club, which she found a bad commercial decision; Williams adds that sponsors forced his television show off.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, I understand with that. You mentioned of course Red Garland. People like Red Garland, Bill Evans, Phineas, people like that . . . and Ahmad. All paid homage to Nat “King” Cole. Was Nat “King” Cole someone that you heard in person very much as a pianist?
Or just after a stand-up vocalist?

Both. I had a lot of records. It seems to me that I heard him on records as a pianist while I was still in Europe. Then I did see him a few times. In fact he came to the London House once, but then I went to see him in a club, Café de Paris or something, in New York. I can’t . . . a supper club. I remember being so upset. People were noisy. I can think of it even today. He’s . . . There’s this wonderful guy, standing up singing, and people are making noise. I think he had to stop and tell them to shut up or keep silent for a minute.
You mentioned he was standing up at this point.
So he had hired a pianist to play for him.
Who was his pianist at that time?
I don’t remember. I honestly don’t.
You were there. Go play piano. [laughs]
I felt . . . I always thought that it was such a terrible thing to do, that they . . . It’s a shame that they did that.
This is one more example of what we alluded to a little earlier.

About the fact of sometimes decisions made by others and not by the artist, and how this can affect the music in the big picture. If a manager or a record- company person said we think it will be up for image and appearance. You should stand and sing, and let’s get someone else to play whatever. Or just because we want to market it a certain way, that affected a lot of things there, the music that he probably wrote and played, because now, he’s not playing for himself, so perhaps he’s not singing the music as challenging, because who’s going to come in practically behind Nat Cole and play piano with that kind of virtuoso artistry?

I wonder how much . . . because naturally, the other person, unless they’re being really coerced, the other person has a chance to say “No, I won’t do that.” Maybe there’s a point at which they think that they are thinking of dollars and furthering their career. Maybe he’s thinking, I’ll get bigger and better, and I’ll get better known, and I’ll be this and that. But to me that really was a bad decision, because here’s that . . . just to see that. He’s standing there singing and not getting the attention he should have. Of course I didn’t see him in a million other places where maybe he did very well. He had a tv show and everything.
Yeah, that only lasted a short while. As you recall, the reason he did leave that show after only two seasons—it was very successful—is because he wasn’t able to get the sponsors.
It was a racial thing, wasn’t it?
